summary: This informational RFC defines concepts and terminology for SIP in a peer-to-peer setting, where the proxy-registrar and routing functions are replaced by a distributed mechanism, such as a distributed hash table. It includes a high-level view of how the parts relate.

plainLanguage.summary: A glossary for phone calls where everyone helps route instead of one central server.

questions: how does overlay network routing work
what is a distributed hash table
subtitle: Shared concepts for phone calls in peer-to-peer networks

tldr.problem: Phone calls traditionally need a central server to find where each person is. In peer-to-peer networks, there is no central server.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines the vocabulary and basic concepts for building peer-to-peer phone systems, where the peers themselves store and look up user locations using a distributed database.
tldr.outcome: These concepts are used by the RELOAD protocol and related P2PSIP standards to enable server-less voice calling, but the terminology may also apply to other distributed applications.

facts.label: Network routing efficiency
facts.value: Maximum log N hops between peers

today: RFC 7890 is an Informational RFC that remains current as a foundational reference for peer-to-peer SIP concepts. It is not obsoleted and continues to serve as the definition of key P2PSIP terminology used by the RELOAD protocol and related standards.

sections.title: The Rendezvous Problem
sections.content:
In traditional phone systems, you dial a number and a central server finds the person you want to call. The challenge is mapping a user's friendly name (like a phone number or email address) to their actual location on the network. This is known as the rendezvous problem.

In conventional SIP networks, this mapping is done by a hierarchy of proxy servers. But in a peer-to-peer approach, instead of having these central proxies, the network participants themselves collectively maintain this information, distributed across the group.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding someone's phone number is easy when you have a switchboard operator. It is harder when everyone is on equal footing and needs to remember each other's numbers.

sections.title: Peer-to-Peer Overlay Architecture
sections.content:
A P2PSIP Overlay is a network where all the nodes are equal peers. The peers together run a distributed database using something like a Distributed Hash Table (DHT), which lets them store and look up user location information. Instead of contacting a proxy server, a peer wanting to call someone uses the overlay to find where that person is located.

Each peer in the overlay can serve multiple roles: it can store user information, forward messages between peers, and provide other services. Some nodes can be Clients that use the overlay without participating in storing data or routing messages. Additionally, some peers can act as gateways between the peer-to-peer network and traditional phone systems or phone devices that do not speak the P2PSIP protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the group keeps pieces of the address book, and they help each other look up phone numbers. Some people just call others without keeping an address book themselves.

sections.title: Core Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC defines several key terms. A Peer is a node that stores information and routes messages. A Node-ID uniquely identifies each peer in the overlay. A User Name is a human-friendly identifier for a person using the system (like a SIP address).

Data in the overlay is organized around Resources, which can be users or services. Each resource has a Resource-ID that is used as a key for storage and lookup. A Resource Record holds information about a resource, such as where a user can be contacted. The Responsible Peer (also called the Root Peer) is the peer that stores a particular resource record.

The distributed database algorithm may use a Distributed Hash Table (DHT), where the hash function determines which peer is responsible for storing each resource. The RFC mentions that RELOAD uses a modified Chord DHT algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Each person has an ID number, a friendly name, and a home address where their information is kept. The address is determined by a math formula so everyone knows who keeps whose information.

sections.title: The Distributed Database Function
sections.content:
The heart of P2PSIP is a distributed database that stores mappings between user names and their contact information. When a user registers with the overlay, their device stores a resource record containing their location. When another user wants to call them, the calling peer looks up the resource record from the peer responsible for storing it.

The RFC describes a simple example: when Peer A wants to call user U, it first looks up the resource record for U from the responsible peer (say Peer Z). This lookup is done using the distributed database algorithm. Once it learns where U is (at Peer A), it can establish a connection to reach the user. The connection itself may be established through intermediate peers if needed to traverse Network Address Translators (NATs).
sections.plainLanguage: To call someone, you ask the peer that knows their address. That peer looks it up and tells you where they are. Then you can call them directly.

sections.title: Joining and Bootstrapping the Overlay
sections.content:
Before a peer can join an overlay, it needs several pieces of information: a Peer-ID to identify itself, configuration details, and optionally credentials to prove it is authorized to join.

To find the overlay, a joining peer first contacts a Bootstrap Server, which is typically a well-known network address that is configured in advance. The Bootstrap Server refers the joining peer to a Bootstrap Peer already in the overlay. The Bootstrap Peer then introduces the joining peer to an Admitting Peer, which helps it join the overlay properly. During this process, peers may authenticate each other using certificates to verify they are legitimate members of the overlay.

The RFC emphasizes that P2PSIP does not mandate how the Peer-ID and credentials are obtained, but the RELOAD protocol specifies the format and mechanisms for getting this information.
sections.plainLanguage: New people joining need someone to introduce them. They ask a known host for an introduction, who points them to someone already in the group. That person helps them learn everyone's addresses and become part of the network.

sections.title: Operating Behind Network Address Translators
sections.content:
Many networks use Network Address Translators (NATs) that can block direct peer-to-peer communication. P2PSIP addresses this by establishing a partial mesh of connections between peers, organized in a structured way based on the distributed database algorithm. When two peers behind NATs need to communicate, the messages are routed through the overlay network along existing connections.

The RFC notes that the structured overlay (typically a DHT) ensures efficient routing: in a network of N peers, any two peers can reach each other in at most log N hops. RELOAD uses techniques like Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) to help peers establish connections across NATs when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Firewalls block direct calls through unknown routes. The network finds paths through connections you already have, so messages still get through.
